title: The speaker and the scene
short: The Florentine friar-painter Filippo Lippi (c. 1406-1469), caught by the night watch near a brothel, talks his way out; a dramatic monologue in blank verse from Men and Women (1855).
body: Browning built the poem on Vasari's Life of Fra Filippo Lippi, which tells how the orphan boy was placed in the Carmelite convent, how he learned from Masaccio's frescoes there, and how his love of women got him into scrapes. The poem is set around 1440 in Florence, at carnival time in spring, past midnight. The guards have seized Lippi at 'an alley's end' among 'sportive ladies'. What follows is a self-defence that becomes a manifesto for realist art. The silent listener is the captain of the watch, whose responses we infer from Lippi's replies. It is blank verse, loose and conversational, full of interruptions and asides.

title: the Carmine
short: Santa Maria del Carmine, the Carmelite church and convent in Florence's Oltrarno, where Lippi was a friar and where Masaccio painted the Brancacci Chapel.
body: Lippi took vows at the Carmine as a boy (Vasari says he entered at eight; records show his profession in 1421). The convent's Brancacci Chapel held the frescoes of Masolino and Masaccio, which Vasari says Lippi studied as a boy. Lippi tells the guards to 'hunt it up' and 'harry out' whatever rat 'haps on his wrong hole'. That is, go and search the convent if you must make a show of zeal. 'Softling' is a soft little thing. The squeaking 'Weke, weke' imitates the mouse.

title: Cosimo de' Medici and the Corner-house
short: Cosimo the Elder (1389-1464), banker and effective ruler of Florence, Lippi's patron; his palace on Via Larga 'caps the corner'.
body: Naming Cosimo instantly changes the guards' manner ('Boh! you were best!'). Lippi is 'lodging' in the Medici palace, later the 'Corner-house' with its great iron rings for flags and horses (ll. 227-30). Vasari tells the story behind the window episode: Cosimo shut Lippi in to make him finish a work, and the painter escaped at night by a rope of bed-sheets to pursue his pleasures. When he returned Cosimo gave him freedom, saying the excellence of rare minds is celestial, not to be driven like a pack-animal. Browning turns the sheets episode into ll. 61-65.

title: the slave with John Baptist's head
short: Lippi sizes up a guard's face as a model for the executioner who holds up the Baptist's head; the painter's eye is always at work.
body: The beheading of John the Baptist at the request of Herodias's daughter is told in Mark 6:17-29 and Matthew 14:3-12. Lippi painted the Feast of Herod in his Prato frescoes. Here the jest has a point: one guard is 'Judas to a tittle' (exactly, to the smallest stroke), and another would serve for the brutal 'slave' with his weapon 'yet unwiped'. Lippi asks for chalk or charcoal ('A wood-coal') to sketch him. The theme of reading faces, learned as a starving child, is introduced here.

title: 'Flower o' the broom' and the street songs
short: Imitations of Tuscan stornelli, three-line folk songs that open by naming a flower and then rhyme on it; Lippi keeps breaking into them.
body: A stornello typically opens with a short line naming a flower ('Fior di ginestra', flower of the broom) and then gives a two-line couplet rhyming with it. Browning, who lived in Florence from 1847, heard such songs in the streets. The fragments recur at moments of feeling (ll. 53-57, 68-69, 110-11, 238-39, 248-49). They give the monologue the sound of carnival and of desire, against the Prior's Latin. Note the self-censored 'You keep your mistr ... manners'. The last, 'Death for us all, and his own life for each!', compresses Lippi's philosophy.

title: the escape by knotted bed-linen
short: Browning's version of Vasari's anecdote: shut up by Cosimo, Lippi tore his bedclothes into a rope and climbed out of the window at night.
body: Vasari reports that Cosimo, wanting Lippi to work, locked him in, and that after two days the painter, driven by his amorous nature, cut his sheets into strips and let himself down from the window. Browning shifts the scene to spring carnival, with three girls laughing in the street like 'the skipping of rabbits by moonlight'. The rapid list of 'Curtain and counterpane and coverlet' and the broken syntax ('a dozen knots, / There was a ladder!') mimic the hurry. 'Hard by Saint Laurence' (l. 67) means near the church of San Lorenzo, the Medici parish church.

title: Jerome and his stone
short: St Jerome in penitence beating his breast with a stone in the desert, a standard subject; Lippi must return to painting self-mortification after a night of pleasure.
body: St Jerome (c. 347-420), translator of the Vulgate, spent years as a hermit in the Syrian desert. Renaissance painters often showed him kneeling, half-naked, striking his chest with a stone 'to subdue the flesh'. The comedy lies in the contrast: the painter returns from chasing girls to paint a saint punishing his body. It points to the poem's main argument, over whether religious art should deny the flesh or celebrate it.

title: Aunt Lapaccia and the convent
short: Vasari's Mona Lapaccia, the aunt who raised the orphan and put him in the Carmine at eight; the boy 'renounces the world' for a mouthful of bread.
body: Vasari says Lippi lost his parents at two, was raised by his aunt Mona Lapaccia, and was sent to the Carmelites at eight. Browning dramatises the moment of vocation as farce: the 'good fat father', wiping his mouth after the meal ('refection-time'), asks whether the boy will 'renounce' the world. The hungry child thinks he means the bread. The list of what he renounces ('Palace, farm, villa, shop, and banking-house') is the Medici's world; the bargain secured him a 'good bellyful', 'warm serge' and 'the rope that goes all round' (the friar's corded belt).

title: the starving boy's education in faces
short: Eight years of begging taught Lippi to read faces and gestures for survival; that hunger-trained observation becomes the realist painter's gift.
body: The passage gives a psychological origin for realism. The boy had to know which passer-by would throw him grapes and which would kick him, which gentleman in a procession would let him catch candle-wax drippings to sell. Which would 'holla for the Eight', the Otto di Guardia, Florence's magistracy for public order and criminal justice. 'Soul and sense of him grow sharp alike': perception and moral understanding develop together. That is the poem's case against the Prior's split between body and soul.

title: Camaldolese and Preaching Friars
short: Rival orders with famous painter-monks: the Camaldolese had Lorenzo Monaco, and the Dominicans (Order of Preachers) had Fra Angelico.
body: The Prior wants a painter for the Carmelites to rival the other orders. The Camaldolese, a Benedictine reform order, had their Florentine house at Santa Maria degli Angeli, where Lorenzo Monaco worked. The 'Preaching Friars' are the Dominicans (Order of Preachers), whose friar-painter was Fra Angelico at San Marco and Fiesole. These are the 'Brother Angelico' and 'Brother Lorenzo' whom the old monks later hold up as the true painters (ll. 235-36). 'Lose a crow and catch a lark' means do not throw away what may turn out valuable.

title: the murderer in sanctuary
short: A killer sits safe at the altar, which gave sanctuary, while his victim's son shakes a fist and crosses himself: Lippi paints church life as it is.
body: Churches traditionally offered sanctuary, so a criminal at the altar could not be seized. Lippi's cloister fresco, as he describes it, is a crowded genre scene: gossips confessing petty thefts ('cribs' of barrel-droppings and candle-ends), children admiring the murderer, the son caught between rage and piety, and a poor girl leaving bread, earrings and flowers. The parenthesis about Christ, 'Whose sad face on the cross sees only this / After the passion of a thousand years', is the poem's sharpest moral comment and comes from realism itself.

title: the Prior's niece
short: A running joke: the Prior's 'niece' (the word suggests a mistress) appears in Lippi's paintings, and he keeps 'correcting' her into Herodias or Saint Lucy.
body: 'Niece' was an old euphemism for a priest's concubine. The simple monks recognise her at once in the fresco ('it's the life!'). The Prior's own objection to the 'white smallish female with the breasts' slips into 'She's just my niece ... Herodias, I would say' (ll. 196-97). Later Lippi compares the angel who rescues him to 'the Prior's niece ... Saint Lucy, I would say' (l. 387). The repeated slip shows the hypocrisy of a Church that denies the body while enjoying it.

title: Giotto
short: Giotto di Bondone (c. 1267-1337), whom the Prior offers as a model of devotional art; for Lippi's age he stood for the older style.
body: Vasari presents Giotto as the founder of modern painting, who turned art toward nature. The Prior, however, cites him as a painter whose saints 'set us praising' without distracting us with 'lines, colors, and what not'. The irony is that Giotto had been the realist of his own day. Victorian taste, encouraged by Ruskin and by Browning's own interest in early Italian art, was rediscovering these 'primitives'. Browning himself collected early Italian panels in Florence.

title: the soul as a new-born babe
short: The Prior stumbles toward the medieval image of the soul as a tiny naked child leaving the dying person's mouth.
body: In medieval painting and sculpture the soul is often shown as a small naked figure leaving the mouth of the dying, received by angels or seized by demons. The Prior tries to define the soul, 'a fire, smoke ... no, it's not ... vapor', and ends with that conventional picture. The comedy is that he can only imagine the soul in bodily form: even orthodox art cannot paint spirit without flesh. Lippi's reply makes the same point as argument.

title: Herodias
short: The Prior confuses Herodias with her daughter, who danced; in Mark it is the daughter (Salome in Josephus) whose dance wins the Baptist's head.
body: In Mark 6:22-25 the daughter of Herodias dances before Herod, and at her mother's prompting asks for John the Baptist's head; Josephus names her Salome. The Prior's slip ('Who went and danced and got men's heads cut off!') turns the girl he admired into a temptress to excuse himself. The confusion was common in tradition. Lippi painted the dancing Salome in the Feast of Herod at Prato.

title: flesh and soul together
short: Lippi's central argument: a painter can 'go a double step', making the body truer and the soul truer at once; beauty itself is God's gift.
body: Against the Prior, who wants 'no more of body than shows soul', Lippi argues that rendering the body truly is a way of rendering spirit. A face that cannot show hope, fear or joy is not beautiful. And if one paints only 'simple beauty and naught else', that is 'about the best thing God invents', and one finds the soul in oneself in giving thanks. Critics usually take this as close to Browning's own view of art, an incarnational aesthetic. Some note that Lippi speaks in self-defence, so the argument is also a sinner's excuse.

title: Brother Angelico and Brother Lorenzo
short: Fra Angelico (c. 1395-1455) and Lorenzo Monaco (c. 1370-c. 1425), monk-painters of a more ideal, devotional style, held up to Lippi as models.
body: The 'old grave eyes' of his teachers still look over his shoulder: 'It's art's decline, my son!' The two monks represent devotional painting of radiant colour and idealised figures. Lippi's 'Fag on at flesh, you'll never make the third!' gives their view: drudge at bodies and you will never join them. Art historians in fact see Lippi absorbing much from Angelico. Browning simplifies the contrast for the drama.

title: Guidi, 'Hulking Tom' (Masaccio)
short: Masaccio (Tommaso, 1401-1428); Browning makes him Lippi's young pupil, though Masaccio was older and Lippi learned from him.
body: 'Masaccio' is a nickname built from Tommaso with a pejorative suffix: roughly 'big, sloppy Tom'. Vasari says it came from his neglect of his dress and affairs. Browning calls him 'Guidi', a surname given him in older sources. In the poem Lippi foresees that this youngster will follow his practice and outdo him. Historically the reverse is true: Masaccio was born about 1401 and died in 1428, and Vasari says Lippi formed his style on Masaccio's Brancacci frescoes. Editors have long noted this as Browning's chronological liberty. The Norton and other notes suggest that Browning followed a disputed tradition, or rearranged history to make Lippi a forerunner of the realism to come.

title: 'Art was given for that'
short: We love things first when we see them painted; art lends the painter's attention to others, so the world 'means intensely, and means good'.
body: Lippi answers the objection that nature is already complete. Painting makes us see what we passed a hundred times, so painted things are 'better to us, / Which is the same thing'. God uses artists to help one another, 'Lending our minds out'. The passage reaches its climax: 'This world's no blot for us, / Nor blank; it means intensely, and means good: / To find its meaning is my meat and drink.' The idea resembles Ruskin's insistence on truth to nature in Modern Painters (1843-60).

title: cullion; phiz
short: 'Cullion' is a base fellow (from Italian coglione); 'phiz' is slang for face (from physiognomy).
body: The captain's 'cullion' is the low fellow among the guards whose 'hanging face' would make a fine study. The word, from Italian coglione, was a coarse insult in Elizabethan English (Shakespeare uses it). 'Phiz', a clipping of 'physiognomy', is the brother's slang in l. 327 for the faces of the painted executioners. Both words keep the talk earthy as the argument rises toward theology.

title: the Saint Laurence at Prato
short: Laurence was roasted on a gridiron; worshippers scratch out the painted torturers' faces in pious rage, which, the brother says, shows the painting works.
body: St Laurence, deacon of Rome, was martyred in 258 by being roasted on a gridiron; legend says he asked to be turned over because one side was done, hence the three slaves 'who turn the Deacon off his toasted side'. Lippi did paint in Prato, where his frescoes in the cathedral choir (1452-65) show the lives of St Stephen and John the Baptist. No Laurence fresco of his at Prato is recorded, and editors treat the detail as Browning's invention or confusion. The anecdote is comic and pointed: realism inflames piety, and the scratching is a sign of 'pity and religion' in the crowd.

title: the picture for Sant' Ambrogio
short: The Coronation of the Virgin (1439-47, now in the Uffizi), painted for the nuns' church of Sant'Ambrogio in Florence; Lippi's 'amends' describes it closely.
body: The altarpiece was paid for from the bequest of Francesco Maringhi, a canon of San Lorenzo and procurator of Sant'Ambrogio, who died in 1441. It shows God the Father crowning the Virgin among angels holding lilies, with St Ambrose and St John the Baptist, patron of Florence, at the sides, and Mary Magdalene and St Eustace with his family among the figures. Lippi's list of saints and the 'bowery, flowery angel-brood' follow the panel. 'Orris-root', powdered iris root, was used as perfume. 'Saint Ambrose, who puts down in black and white / The convent's friends' jokes on the saint as recorder of benefactors' names.

title: Job, 'the man of Uz'
short: Job 1:1, 'a man in the land of Uz'; the pun 'Us without the z' makes Job the patron of painters who need his patience.
body: The Book of Job opens: 'There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job' (Job 1:1). Job's patience became proverbial (James 5:11). Lippi's pun turns Uz into 'Us', the painters who need patience with patrons and Priors. Modern descriptions of the panel name Ambrose, John the Baptist, Mary Magdalene and Eustace, not Job, so Lippi's 'past mistake' may be Browning's own addition or identification.

title: 'Iste perfecit opus!'
short: The Latin on an angel's scroll in the Coronation; Browning takes the figure beside it as Lippi's self-portrait, though it is now generally thought to be the commissioner, Maringhi.
body: In the painting an angel holds a cartouche inscribed 'ISTE PERFECIT OPUS' facing a kneeling cleric. Vasari and nineteenth-century viewers took the figure for Lippi himself. Browning dramatises this: the painter, caught 'by mistake' among the saints, is defended by a 'sweet angelic slip of a thing' who says, in effect, he made you. Modern art historians generally think the figure is the patron, Francesco Maringhi, and that the scroll means 'this man commissioned the work'. Lippi's own self-portrait is usually identified in a separate Carmelite figure on the left. Browning's reading suits his theme: the artist's humble creativity is blessed in the sacred scene.

title: Saint Lucy
short: St Lucy of Syracuse, virgin martyr, patron of eyesight; Lippi again slips and corrects 'the Prior's niece' into a saint.
body: Lucy (d. 304) is patron saint of the eyes, often painted holding her eyes on a dish. Her name means 'light'. The slip echoes the Prior's 'my niece ... Herodias': this time Lippi makes the girl a saint, not a temptress. It sums up his art, which finds holiness in real women's faces. Biographies record that Lippi later had a relationship with a nun, Lucrezia Buti, at Prato, and their son Filippino became a painter. Browning's poem only hints at this future.
